source.question: e-9949
source.value:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at $\theta=\dfrac\pi4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $2$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{2}+2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}+2}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: e-10034
source.value:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r = 2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /3} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r=\theta,$ we get

$$
x = \theta\cos\theta, \qquad y=\theta\sin\theta.
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta)\mathbin{:}$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =(\theta )^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$
